Question Choices: Six donut-tree types are available for two labeled planting spots. The two trees must have different types. How many ordered plantings are possible? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: The spots are labeled, so JL and LJ are different;Choose the first type, then a different second type
Solution: There are 6 choices for the first spot and 5 remaining choices for the second.;The ordered count is $P(6,2)=6\cdot5=30$.

Question Choices: Six donut-tree types are available for two labeled planting spots, and the same type may be used twice. How many ordered plantings are possible? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: There are 6 choices for each labeled spot;You can also split into different-type and same-type cases
Solution: There are $6\cdot6=36$ ordered plantings.;Equivalently, there are $P(6,2)=30$ off-diagonal choices and $P(6,1)=6$ same-type choices, for $30+6=36$.

Question Choices: Two different donut-tree types are selected from 6 types, and order does not matter. How many selections are possible? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: JL and LJ now count as the same selection;Use $C(6,2)$
Solution: $C(6,2)=\dfrac{6!}{4!2!}=15$ unordered selections of two distinct types.

Question Choices: Two donut-tree types are selected from 6 types, order does not matter, and the same type may be selected twice. How many selections are possible? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: Split the selections into two different types and two matching types;Use $C(6,2)$ for different types and $C(6,1)$ for matching types
Solution: There are $C(6,2)=15$ selections with two different types and $C(6,1)=6$ selections with matching types.;The total is $15+6=21$.

Question Choices: Use Pascal's identity to evaluate C(9,4)+C(9,3). Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: Pascal's identity says $C(n,k)=C(n-1,k)+C(n-1,k-1)$;Match the two terms to one larger binomial coefficient
Solution: By Pascal's identity, $C(9,4)+C(9,3)=C(10,4)$.;Therefore the value is $210$.

Question Choices: There are C(7,3)=35 unordered groups of 3 objects. How many ordered selections of 3 objects are there? Input C(... ...) and P(... ...) for combination and permutation.
Hints: Each unordered group of 3 objects has 3! orders;Multiply 35 by 3!
Solution: Each of the $C(7,3)=35$ groups can be ordered in $3!=6$ ways.;Thus $P(7,3)=35\cdot6=210$.
